Day 1. Over dinner in their flat, Jahnavi's flatmate Nirmala rolled her eyes at the news. “Everyone who doesn't agree with us is a sheep,” Nirmala said, a phrase Jahnavi had never heard her use. Their third flatmate laughed uneasily.
Day 9. Nirmala cancelled the weekend trip. “The group needs me online.” Her replies at breakfast were clipped.
Day 20. Instead of scolding, Jahnavi asked, “What's the group like? What do you enjoy there?” Nirmala talked for twenty minutes. Jahnavi listened, then suggested a walk on Sunday. She added, “If it keeps going and you feel really low or stuck, I'd like you to talk to someone qualified, and I'll come along.”

qa.a: Jahnavi was probably surprised and uneasy, since it was a phrase Jahnavi had never heard Nirmala use.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi choose on Day 20 instead of scolding, and what did it lead to?
qa.a: Jahnavi asked curious questions and listened, so Nirmala talked for twenty minutes, and then Jahnavi suggested a walk and offered to go along to someone qualified if things kept going.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Nirmala to be asked, “What do you enjoy there?” instead of being scolded?
qa.a: Nirmala may have felt surprised and relieved to be heard, which fits talking for twenty minutes and then agreeing to a walk.

passage: “Beta, I'll tell you what I did when my sister Usha was seventeen,” said Manoj. “I was twenty-five and living at home. Usha spent hours in an online group about one cause. Her words began to change. Everything became 'traitors' and 'idiots.' She snapped at Amma when Amma asked about dinner. Our father wanted to take her phone. I said, 'Give me a week.' I asked Usha, 'What do you like about that group?' She stared at me. Then she talked for an hour: they had welcomed her when school had been lonely. I said, 'That matters. Show me something you read there and I'll show you something I read.' It took months. If she had stopped eating or sleeping, I would have taken her to a doctor. But she started laughing at dinner again.”

qa.q: How old was Usha in the story?
qa.a: Usha was seventeen.

qa.q: What did Manoj want for Usha when Manoj said, “Give me a week”?
qa.a: Manoj was worried about Usha and wanted Usha to feel listened to and not punished, hoping to understand the pull of the group before anyone took the phone away.

qa.q: What choice by Manoj replaced the idea of taking the phone?
qa.a: Manoj asked the father for a week and asked Usha what she liked about the group, listening and trading readings with her instead of confiscating.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Usha to be asked, ‘What do you like about that group?’ instead of having the phone taken?
qa.a: Usha was probably surprised and guarded at first, expecting a scolding, and may have felt relieved to be asked with curiosity.

grounding: A sibling sees a sister's language and mood harden after hours in an online group, and curiosity works better than confiscation.

passage: Chaitanya and Jatin shared a one-room flat in Pune and a looming job deadline, so Chaitanya noticed the change fast. Jatin, who used to joke about everything, now stayed up till three in a forum that blamed 'outsiders' for every problem in the city. His words changed: people became 'those types'. One night, when a delivery rider was late, Jatin swore at him in a way that made Chaitanya's stomach turn. Chaitanya wanted to shout, or unplug the router. Instead, the next morning over chai, he asked, 'What's that forum giving you that we're not?' Jatin was quiet, then said, 'Everyone there gets how unfair things are.' They talked for an hour. Chaitanya didn't win the argument. But he suggested they both see the college counsellor about job stress, and on Thursday Jatin went.

qa.q: Till what time did Jatin stay up in the forum?
qa.a: Till three.

qa.q: How did Chaitanya feel when Jatin swore at the delivery rider?
qa.a: Chaitanya felt sick and alarmed, stomach turning, tempted to shout or unplug the router.

qa.q: Why was Chaitanya's morning question wiser than unplugging the router?
qa.a: Asking what the forum gave Jatin opened a real conversation and led to the counsellor, while confiscating would likely have pushed Jatin away.

qa.q: What does Jatin seem to be getting from the forum?
qa.a: A feeling of being understood about how unfair things are, which hints at stress and loneliness behind the harder language.

grounding: A flatmate notices a friend's language harden after hours in an online group and chooses curiosity and a counsellor over confiscation.

passage: In their Chennai flat, Uma noticed it first in small words. Her son Dhruv began calling people 'weak' and 'soft', even his cousin, who had a newborn and couldn't get to the gym. He spent his evenings in an online fitness group, headphones on. He skipped the family's Sunday biryani and snapped at his father for offering him a plate. Uma's first thought was to take his phone, as she might have when he was twelve. She didn't. On Tuesday she asked him to walk with her to the vegetable market and asked, 'What do you like about that group?' He talked for twenty minutes. Some of it worried her more. That night, calmly, she told him she was concerned about the skipped meals and asked if he would see their family doctor with her. After a long pause, he said yes.

qa.q: What did Uma ask Dhruv on the walk?
qa.a: 'What do you like about that group?'

qa.q: What was Uma feeling when she noticed Dhruv's new words and skipped meals?
qa.a: She felt worried and alarmed, and was tempted to take his phone as she might have when he was younger.

qa.q: What made Uma's approach wise?
qa.a: She chose curiosity and a calm talk over confiscation, listened, then named her specific concern and suggested seeing the family doctor together.

qa.q: How might Dhruv's cousin feel being called 'soft'?
qa.a: Probably hurt and judged, since a newborn, not weakness, kept the cousin away from the gym.

grounding: A parent notices a grown son's language and mood harden in an online group and uses conversation and a doctor rather than confiscation.

'You've said "everyone's fake" four times this evening,' Hansa said, pouring tea.
Afreen didn't look up from her phone. 'Because they are. You should see this group. They expose people's fake lives every day.'
'You were up till four again. I heard you.'
'So?'
'So you seem angry all the time. And you used to love weddings. You called Rukhsana's reception "a performance".'
Afreen put the phone down. 'It was.'
'Was it? Or is that the group talking?' Hansa sat beside her. 'I'm not going to lecture you. I just miss you. What does the group give you?'
Afreen was quiet for a long time. 'I don't feel left out there. Everyone's laughing at the same people.'
'Will you come for a walk tomorrow, no phones? Just us?'
'...Fine. One walk.'

qa.q: Until what time was Afreen up again?
qa.a: Till four.

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling as she counted Afreen's 'everyone's fake' comments?
qa.a: Hansa felt worried and sad, missing the friend who used to love weddings.

qa.q: What did Hansa do that helped Afreen open up?
qa.a: She avoided lecturing, said she missed Afreen, asked what the group gave her, and suggested a phone-free walk.

qa.q: What does Afreen seem to get from the group?
qa.a: A sense of not being left out, since everyone laughs at the same people, which hints at loneliness behind the anger.

grounding: A friend notices someone's mood harden after hours in an online group and responds with curiosity and time together.

subtopic: Online communities, echo chambers and moderation

passage: I'm Kunal, and I first noticed it in Rekha's jokes. We had shared a flat since college, and she used to laugh at everything, including herself. Around March she started spending evenings in an online group that mocked people it called "soft", earphones in till two. Her jokes about the neighbours got meaner. At dinner with Farah and Joseph she called a colleague "one of those", and the table went quiet. My first instinct was to lecture her, or tell her to delete the app. I didn't. One Sunday I just asked, "What do you like about that group?" She talked for an hour, about feeling lonely after her promotion fell through, about people who "got" her. I listened. Then I said, gently, that the Rekha I knew didn't talk about people like that. Last week she asked me for the number of the counsellor I'd seen last year.

qa.q: How late did Rekha stay in the group with earphones in?
qa.a: Earphones in till two.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling when the dinner table went quiet?
qa.a: Kunal was worried and uneasy, and tempted to lecture Rekha or tell her to delete the app.

qa.q: Why did Kunal's question work better than a lecture?
qa.a: Asking what Rekha liked about the group let her talk about her loneliness, and listening first made the gentle, honest remark easier to hear.

qa.q: What had the group been giving Rekha, from her side?
qa.a: It seemed to ease her loneliness after the promotion fell through, offering people who "got" her.

grounding: Kunal notices a friend's language harden after hours in an online group, chooses curiosity over confiscation, and she turns to a counsellor.
